Part 1 SA S92A-RFM-006
Introduction
PART 1
INTRODUCTION
The S-92 helicopter may be delivered with optional engines and equipment for ditching, external
lift, search and rescue, and other types of operation. To reduce the need for flight manual
supplements, major configuration differences are addressed by issuing different versions of the
flight manual. These configuration differences are identified in the flight manual by icons.
Operators must ensure that the applicable FAA-approved flight manual is in the aircraft. Sikorsky
document SA S92A-FMCD-000 specifies the applicable flight manual number for each aircraft.
The applicable flight manual number may change because of aircraft modifications. This document
will be revised to indicate such changes and to add new aircraft. The current revision of SA
S92A-FMCD-000 can be obtained from Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation or from the Manager,
Boston Aircraft Certification Office.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
Revised: March 16, 2007

PART 1, SECTION I
OPERATING LIMITATIONS
GENERAL
NOTE
Compliance with the limitations in this section is mandatory.
BASIS OF CERTIFICATION
This helicopter is certified in accordance with FAR Part 29 Category ’A’ and Category ’B’ requirements.
TYPES OF OPERATION
Category ’A’ with a maximum of 19 passenger seats or Category ’B’ with 9 or less passenger seats; Day, Night, VFR and IFR.
RIPS Flight in icing conditions up to 10,000 feet pressure altitude with Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS) installed.
REQUIRED EQUIPMENT
The following equipment must be operational:
1. Auxiliary Power unit.
2. Two Data Concentrator Units (DCUs) (IMC).
3. Four instrument panel Multifunction Displays (MFDs) configured as follows:
v PFD mode selected on both outboard displays.
v EICAS mode selected on one inboard display.
4. AFCS:
v Day or night, IFR or VFR - (Normal Operations):
- PSAS1 and PSAS2, AP1 and AP2, ATT Mode, cyclic and rudder trim. Maximum V NE is 165 KIAS.
v Day or night, VFR (With certain PSAS and/or AP components inoperative):
- PSAS1 and PSAS2, AP1 or AP2, ATT Mode, cyclic and rudder trim. Maximum V NE is 165 KIAS.
- PSAS1 and PSAS2, AP1 and/or AP2, SAS Mode, cyclic and rudder trim. Maximum V NE is 165 KIAS.
- PSAS1 or PSAS2, AP1 and AP2, ATT Mode, cyclic and rudder trim. Maximum V NE is 120 KIAS.
- PSAS1/AP1 or PSAS2/AP2, SAS Mode, functional cyclic trim release. Maximum V is 120 KIAS.
NE

OPERATING LIMITATIONS
CAUTION
When operating in a degraded AFCS mode, a pilot will be
attentive to the flight controls when in ATT mode and will
manually control the aircraft when flying in SAS mode.
NOTE
Takeoff with a secondary SAS engaged is not authorized. Secondary
SAS may be engaged after an inflight failure of a primary SAS
computer.
5. Two primary AC generators (IMC).
6. All standby instruments (IMC).
7. The applicable operators manual must be carried on board the aircraft for all equipment that is not covered in Part II
of this manual.
MINIMUM FLIGHT CREW
Two pilots. For the procedures in this manual the 9 pilot 9 occupies the right cockpit seat and the 9 copilot 9 occupies the left
cockpit seat. The Pilot in Command (PIC) may occupy either cockpit seat.
ENHANCED GROUND PROXIMITY WARNING SYSTEM (EGPWS)
The EGPWS will not provide power line warnings. Power lines are not included in the EGPWS data base.
1. Navigation must not be predicated upon the use of EGPWS information.
NOTE
The Terrain and Obstacle display is intended to serve as a terrain and
obstacle awareness tool only. The display and/or database may not
provide the accuracy and/or fidelity on which to base routine navigation
decisions and plan routes to avoid terrain or obstacles.
2. EGPWS Low Altitude Mode must not be selected when operating under IMC conditions except as required when
performing offshore platform IMC Approach Procedures or other Special Procedures.
DIGITAL MAP
Do not use the EuroNav Digital Map system for primary navigation.

SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section I
OPERATING LIMITATIONS
FLIGHT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (FMS)
FMS OPERATIONAL APPROVALS
The UNS-1Esp Flight Management System (FMS) has been demonstrated capable of, and been shown to meet the
requirements for the following operations:
1. VFR/IFR enroute, terminal and instrument approach (GPS stand-alone and GPS overlay VOR, VOR-DME, NDB, and
RNAV) operation within the U.S. National Airspace System using the WGS-84 coordinate reference datum. Satellite
navigation is based upon use of only the Global Positioning System (GPS) operated by the United States.
2. RNP5/BRNAV - Provided it is receiving usable navigation information from one or more of the following:
a. GPS
b. One VOR/DME or multiple DMEs.
3. Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Enroute, Terminal, and Approach operations, provided the FMS is receiving usable
navigation information.
NOTE
Use of P-ILS mode is authorized to provide vertical guidance during
GPS based instrument approach procedures.
4. Use of Barometric VNAV to conduct RNAV instrument approach procedures published with a VNAV Decision Altitude
(LNAV/VNAV minimums).
FMS OPERATING LIMITATIONS
GENERAL
1. The software status stated in the UNS-1Esp Pilot’s Guide, Report No. 2423sv802/902, dated 16 September 2003, or later
approved revision, must match that displayed on the equipment.
2. When latitude/longitude transferred from the internal database (IDB) is displayed on the CDU, the pilot will ensure that
it is a reasonable position for the requested identifier.
3. The internal database (IDB) must be updated to the latest revision every 28 days; updating to be accomplished with the
Universal Avionics update disk or equivalent.
4. The fuel management mode is for advisory purposes only and it does not replace the aircraft primary fuel flow and fuel
quantity systems.
5. When operating north of 73 degrees north latitude or south of 60 degrees south latitude the pilot must manually insert
magnetic variation.
6. When the air data input is lost to the FMS, the pilot must manually insert TAS and Altitude information every 10
minutes.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
Revised: June 18, 2010

=== DOC PAGE 29 ===
Part 1, Section I SA S92A-RFM-006
OPERATING LIMITATIONS
7. IFR En Route and Terminal navigation are prohibited unless the pilot verifies the currency of the data base or verifies
each selected Waypoint for accuracy by reference to current approved data.
8. Other navigation equipment appropriate to the ground facilities along the intended route must be installed and operable,
as required by the operating rules applicable to the specific type of operation (i.e. VOR, DME, etc.).
FMS LNAV OPERATION
1. Navigation shall not be predicated upon the UNS-1Esp during periods of dead reckoning (DR).
2. Following a period of dead reckoning, position should be verified by visually sighting ground reference points and/or
by using other navigation equipment such as NDB, VOR, DME, or radar fix.
3. The use of manually inserted runway coordinates is limited to VFR operations.
FMS VNAV OPERATIONS
1. If VNAV is to be used for approach, use of enroute VNAV must be discontinued within 10 nm of the FAF. When the
approach mode is activated, as indicated by a green APP on the PFD, VNAV may be armed for the approach.
2. Pilot and Co-pilot altimeters are the primary altitude reference during all VNAV operations.
FMS APPROACHES
1. Instrument approaches must be accomplished in accordance with approved instrument approach procedures that are
retrieved from the FMS navigation data base. The FMS database must incorporate the current update cycle.
NOTE
Not all published approaches are in the FMS database. The flight crew
must ensure that the planned approach is in the database.
2. When using FMS guidance for conducting instrument approach procedures that do not include 9 GPS 9 or 9 RNAV 9 in the
title of the published procedure, unless otherwise authorized by local authority, the flight crew must verify that the
procedure-specified navaid and associated avionics are operational.
3. If an 9 INTEG 9 message is displayed on the PFD during an approach, navigation predicated on GPS should be
discontinued.
4. Instrument approaches must be conducted in the approach mode of operation prior to the FAF as indicated by a green
APP on the PFD.
5. RAIM must be available at the final approach fix in order to accomplish GPS based non-precision approaches.When
RAIM is not available, 9 INTEG 9 will be displayed on the PFD and 9 NO GPS RAIM @ FAF 9 or 9 NO GPS @ MAP 9
messages will be displayed on the UNS-1 CDU.
6. Operation in accordance with GLS approach minimums and other operations requiring WAAS are not approved.
7. ILS, LOC, LOC-BC, LDA, SDF, and MLS approaches are not authorized.
8. The UNS-1Esp is approved for FMS VFR approaches as a VFR pilot aid only.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005

OPERATING LIMITATIONS
FLIGHT LIMITS
See Figure 1-1 for altitude and airspeeds to be avoided in the event of an engine failure.
Category 9 A 9 ground level helipad takeoffs and landings will be flown in accordance with the Category 9 A 9 procedures listed
in Section II of this manual and within the Category 9 A 9 weight, altitude and temperature limits shown in Section IV of this
manual. See Figure 4-17 for Category 9 A 9 ground level helipad maximum takeoff gross weight and Figure 4-21 for Category
9 A 9 ground level helipad maximum landing gross weight. Minimum helipad size for Category 9 A 9 ground level helipad
operations is a 102 foot square.
Aerobatic maneuvers are prohibited.
Practice touchdown autorotations are prohibited.
360° hovering turns in less than 12 seconds are prohibited.
Flight in freezing drizzle/freezing rain/supercooled large drops (SLD) is prohibited.
For flight into icing conditions, the Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS) must be turned on.
Use of OEI engine power ratings except in the event of an actual engine failure is prohibited.
Category 9 A 9 horizontal takeoffs and landings are limited to 35 knots of crosswind component or less. Category 9 A 9 ground
level helipad takeoffs and landings are limited to 22 knots of crosswind component or less.
Maximum bank angle with one primary flight control servo inoperative is 30°.
With low fuel light(s) illuminated, avoid steady state pitch attitudes in excess of 10° nose up and lower than 5° nose down.
Slope landing limits are 10° nose up or down slope, 13° left or right side of the aircraft up slope.
Flight with the ramp, airstair door or cabin windows open is prohibited. The opening of cockpit windows in flight is authorized
provided the window can be latched fully open and loose equipment is secured in the cockpit.
Carriage of passengers is prohibited with the installation of the lower search/rescue door.
Flight with the upper cabin sliding door and the lower (inward opening) SAR door open is authorized provided loose
equipment is secured in the cabin and applicable airspeed limits are observed.
CAUTION
Prior to inflight operations with a cabin door open, all cabin
occupants must be seated with a seat belt fastened or
restrained with an approved and properly adjusted harness.
Maximum pitch attitude for opening or closing the upper sliding door is 10° nose up or down. Maximum bank angle for
opening or closing the upper sliding door is 30°.
Maximum demonstrated night Category 9 A 9 vertical Takeoff Decision Point (TDP) is 110 feet.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005

SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section I
OPERATING LIMITATIONS
FLOAT Arming or deploying the life rafts in flight is prohibited.
FLOAT Deploying the floats in flight is prohibited.
The maximum demonstrated IFR approach gradient for airspeeds above 90 KIAS is 4.0°. The maximum demonstrated IFR
approach gradient for airspeeds at or below 90 KIAS is 7.0°.
AIRSPEED LIMITS
V NE power on (maximum airspeed) is 165 KIAS.
NOTE
The air data computers automatically calculate V NE as a function of
temperature, pressure altitude and gross weight for display on the
airspeed indicator (PFD display mode).
Maximum airspeed with the landing gear down or in transit is 165 KIAS.
Maximum airspeed with the APU operating is 150 KIAS.
V NE power off is 120 KIAS. If V NE power on is less than 120 KIAS, the lower V NE shall apply for the power off case as well.
Maximum airspeed with one engine inoperative is 120 KIAS.
Maximum airspeed with one or both SAS inoperative is 120 KIAS.
Maximum airspeed with both APs inoperative is 120 KIAS.
Maximum airspeed with one primary flight control servo inoperative is 120 KIAS.
Maximum airspeed with the hydraulic boost inoperative is 120 KIAS.
Maximum airspeed with any sliding door or window pinned open is 120 KIAS. This includes the upper sliding SAR
doors/windows, the inward opening lower door, and the full length sliding door.
Maximum airspeed for activation of the landing gear emergency blowdown is 90 KIAS.
Maximum airspeed for opening or closing any sliding door or window is 80 KIAS. This includes the upper sliding SAR
doors/windows, the inward opening lower door, and the full length sliding door.
FLOAT Maximum airspeed with floats armed is 80 KIAS.
Maximum groundspeed for landing or takeoff is 65 knots.
V mini (minimum airspeed for instrument flight) is 50 KIAS.
FLOAT Maximum airspeed after inadvertent float deployment is 50 KIAS in a climb, 55 KIAS in level flight, and 60 KIAS
in descent/autorotation.

=== DOC PAGE 35 ===
Part 1, Section I SA S92A-RFM-006
OPERATING LIMITATIONS
Maximum airspeed for standard windshield wiper operations is 40 knots. Maximum airspeed for improved windshield wiper
operations is 100 KIAS.
NOTE
The main wiper arm of a standard windshield wiper (P/N 92207-01807-
103) is U-shaped, with the opening of the 9 U 9 visible from the cockpit.
The improved wiper arm (P/N 92207-01807-114) includes a stiffener
inside the 9 U, 9 which is visible from the cockpit.
Maximum airspeed for sideward flight or crosswind hover is 35 knots.
Maximum airspeed for rearward flight or tailwind hover is 35 knots.
Maximum groundspeed for taxi operations is 35 knots.
Maximum groundspeed for brake application is 35 knots.
ALTITUDE LIMITS
Takeoff and landing: See Figures 1-2 and 1-3.
Enroute: 15,000 feet density altitude.
Maximum altitude for Category 9 A 9 ground level helipad operations is 5,500 feet density altitude or 6,000 feet pressure
altitude, whichever is lower.
Minimum altitude for coupled operations with airspeed above 120 KIAS is 200 feet AGL.
Minimum altitude for coupled operations with airspeed at or below 120 KIAS is 50 feet AGL. When coupled below 200 feet
AGL, the pilot will monitor the flight controls and take action in the event of an excessive rate of descent. Coupled flight below
100 feet AGL will be in visual meteorological conditions.
RIPS Flight in icing conditions: 10,000 feet pressure altitude.
AMBIENT TEMPERATURE LIMITS
-40°C to ISA +35°C. Operation is prohibited if the rotorcraft, with its engines shut down, is exposed to a ground ambient
temperature below -25°C for a period longer than 1 hour. To restore the rotorcraft to airworthy status it should be warmed at
or above a temperature of 0°C (+32°F) for 8 hours or; Cold Weather Pre-heat kit, Part Number 92700-00110-011, must be
utilized in accordance with the Rotorcraft Flight Manual Cold Weather Procedures.
Pitot heat and engine anti-ice should be turned on when OAT is less than 5°C.
ENVIRONMENTAL CONTROL SYSTEM LIMITS
To assure adequate fresh air ventilation to the cockpit when operating the air-conditioning system in flight, the cockpit
temperature Mode selection switch shall not be placed in the MAX ACS or recirculation position. The air-conditioning MAX
ACS position is to be used on the ground only. If neither heat nor air-conditioning is used in flight, the cockpit vent must be
on.

WEIGHT LIMITS
Maximum takeoff and landing weight is 26,500 pounds (12,020 kilograms). Minimum operating weight is 16,200 pounds
(7,348 kilograms). This helicopter is to be operated using the approved loading schedule. See LOADING INFORMATION
in RFM Part 2, Section II.

SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section I
OPERATING LIMITATIONS
CAUTION
Imbalances in excess of 700 pounds (317 kilograms) between
fuel tanks, when combined with grossly unbalanced
cargo/passenger loading, may put the aircraft outside of
allowable lateral CG limits.
CABIN FLOOR LOADING LIMITS
Maximum allowable cabin floor loading is 75 pounds per square foot (366 Kg per square meter). If the helicopter is equipped
with a heavy duty floor, the maximum loading is 200 pounds per square foot (976 Kg per square meter).
CAUTION
Care must be exercised to be sure that passenger, baggage,
and fuel loading does not cause aircraft maximum gross
weight and/or CG limits to be exceeded.
BAGGAGE LOADING LIMIT
When the rear ramp area is configured for stowing baggage (aft cabin cargo bulkhead and shelf installed), the maximum
combined load is 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms). The maximum shelf load is 300 pounds (136 kilograms). The maximum floor
ramp load is 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms). Maximum floor loading on the ramp is 200 pounds per square foot (976.5
kilograms per square meter).
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
Revised: June 11, 2006

NORMAL PROCEDURES
*STARTING ENGINES
1. NO. 1 AND NO. 2 FUEL — As required (XFD for fi rst start of day).
2. ENG IGN NO 1 and NO 2 — AUTO.
3. Rotor brake — As required.
4. Fire guard — POSTED (if available).
5. Rotor blades — CLEAR.
NOTE
Prior to rotor engagement, the collective will rest in a mid-range
position. Monitor collective position during initial rotor engagement. As
N increases through approximately 20% and hydraulic pressure
r
increases, depress the collective trim switch and move the collective to
the full down position. Avoid using the collective trim switch until
hydraulic pressure builds.
CAUTION
Avoid prolonged periods with N r between the ranges of 36 to
49% and 56 to 67%.
CAUTION
Restarting a hot engine that was not properly cooled for 2
minutes may cause a bowed compressor rotor and rubs of
airfoils and seals. The damage is cumulative and may result
in future hot starts.
6. #1 Engine — START.
NOTE
Both engines may be started simultaneously when the OAT is below
25 ° C at sea level. Decrease allowable OAT 2 ° C per one thousand feet of
altitude.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
2-14 Revised: April 21, 2009

NOTE
FADEC 5.21 includes an automatic blow down feature which will
prevent engine start until TGT decreases below 150 ° C when the throttle

The inability to cool the engine below 150 ° C during a start attempt may
be an indication of an engine or start system malfunction.

When moving the throttle from IDLE to STOP, move the throttle
quickly. Allowing the throttle to dwell in excess of three seconds in an
intermediate position between IDLE and STOP may cause an ENG 1-2
OVSP TEST caution.
NOTE
To ensure proper power turbine cooling, run the engines at idle speed for
a minimum of 2 minutes before shutdown. Cooling the engine at IDLE
significantly reduces the chance of hot starts and engine seal rubs. If
running for 2 minutes at IDLE is not possible for operational reasons,
run the engines below 90% N g for at least 2 minutes prior to shutdown,
including at least 60 seconds at IDLE.
If the engine was not cooled for 2 minutes prior to shutdown (emergency shutdown), do the following:
a. Motor the engine for 1 minute and until TGT is less than 150°C.

SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section II
NORMAL PROCEDURES
QUICK LAUNCH PROCEDURES
The following procedures allow the operator to prepare the aircraft for immediate launch. This will allow the aircrew to start
the engines and launch in a minimum amount of time. Prior to assuming a quick launch status, the helicopter will be run-up
to include completion of the following checks:
BEFORE STARTING ENGINES
COCKPIT EQUIPMENT CHECKS
STARTING ENGINES
ROTOR ENGAGEMENT AND ENGINE RUNUP
AFTER LANDING
SHUTDOWN
A helicopter that is to be prepared for a quick launch immediately after shutdown, following a flight, is considered to have
all required checklists completed up to the Alert Checklist.
NOTE
The quick launch procedures will only be used when no maintenance
has been accomplished after the Alert Checklist is completed. Ensure
proper fuel loading for the mission.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
Revised: July 17, 2007

NORMAL PROCEDURES
TAKEOFF AND LANDING PROCEDURES
Category 9 A 9 takeoff and landing procedures, when accomplished at the approved weight, altitude, temperature, field length,
and wind conditions, guarantee continued safe flight and landing after an engine failure. When operating outside of the
approved Category 9 A 9 procedures, weight, and ambient conditions, continued safe flight and landing after an engine failure
is not guaranteed.
Pilot duties: The Category 9 A 9 takeoff and landing maneuvers may be flown from either the pilot or copilot seat. These
maneuvers utilize outside references supplemented by the cockpit instruments. The procedures require adherence to specific
airspeeds, power settings, pitch attitudes, climb/descent rates and rotor speeds. The Flying Pilot (FP) should concentrate on
outside references with occasional cross checks of the PFD to ensure that performance parameters are met. The Non-Flying
Pilot (NFP) should aid the FP by announcing decision points and providing verbal guidance when errors occur in performance
parameters and/or flight path.
The following are examples of NFP duties. These examples are not exhaustive. Specific duties and standardized calls should
be developed by each operator to support specific flying environments and operations.
1. During all procedures, announce when the aircraft attains the Takeoff Decision Point (TDP) or Landing Decision Point
(LDP) airspeed and/or altitude.
2. During vertical takeoffs, announce when the actual rate of climb deviates significantly from the desired rate of climb.
3. During OEI rejected vertical takeoffs and all continued takeoffs, announce when the actual N r is outside of the desired
range for the maneuver (i.e., not between 100 and 104%).
4. During fly-away maneuvers, announce when V toss is attained and, subsequently, if airspeed falls below V toss .
5. During OEI vertical land back maneuvers, announce when the actual ground track deviates from the desired ground
track.

NORMAL PROCEDURES
COLD WEATHER PROCEDURES
With normal servicing, the aircraft can operate at temperatures down to -40°C. Preheat must be used at temperatures below
-25°C.
PRE-HEAT
If the aircraft has been parked in ambient temperatures at or below -25°C for 4 hours or longer, the main rotor head and main
rotor flight control servos must be pre-heated prior to aircraft operation. The pre-heat kit, P/N 92700-00110-011, shall be
installed. The proper installation encloses the area from just below the bifilar outboard to the main rotor blade cuffs, and then
back in to the base of the main flight control servos. Pre-heat air from standard ground support equipment (Herman Nelson)
shall be directed into the area enclosed by the pre-heat kit. Set pre-heat air temperature to approximately 130°F. Pre-heating
shall be started a minimum of 1 hour before operation is started to give components time to warm up.
CAUTION
Failure to pre-heat may result in excessive fluid leakage from
the main rotor dampers and flight control servos.
COLD WEATHER PRE-FLIGHT CHECK
In addition to the standard exterior check items, the aircraft must be inspected for accumulated ice and/or snow. Particular
attention should be paid to the main rotor head and blades, tail rotor, flight controls, engine inlets, and steps.
CAUTION
Any accumulations of ice or snow must be removed with
heated air or an approved de-icing fluid prior to starting the
aircraft. Failure to do so may result in significant degradation
of flying qualities or performance, unwanted structural ef-
fects in flight, or foreign object damage if ice is ingested into
an engine.
CAUTION
Never remove accumulated ice by scraping or chipping.
Remove ice by applying heat or an approved de-icing fluid.
Main rotor blade covers should be used if the aircraft is to
remain outside overnight.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005

NORMAL PROCEDURES
COLD WEATHER CONTROL EXERCISE
A cold weather warm-up exercise must be accomplished when the aircraft is to be operated at temperatures at or below -17°C.
Exercise collective independently of the rudder pedals.
1. At temperatures between -17°C and -31°C, move the fight controls for 1 minute as follows:
a. Position the collective at approximately mid position. Slowly move the collective alternately up and down
approximately 1 1/2 inches of travel from the mid position to complete 30 cycles in 1 minute.
b. Slowly move each rudder pedal alternately through approximately 3/4 inch of travel from the neutral position to
complete 30 cycles in 1 minute.
2. At temperatures between -31°C and -40°C, move the flight controls for 2 minutes as follows:
a. Move the collective alternately up and down approximately 3/4 inch of travel from the mid position during the first
minute, and 1 1/2 inches of travel during the second minute.
b. Move each rudder pedal alternately through approximately 3/8 inch of travel from neutral during the first minute, and
3/4 inch during the second minute.
LEAK DETECTION AND ISOLATION (LDI) TEST
If the LDI test is accomplished on a cold soaked aircraft, the test result may show 9 TEST INHIBITED 9 . In this case, continue
with all cold weather procedures and warm the hydraulic system at 50% N r . Repeat the test with a warm hydraulic system.
When operating in an extreme cold weather environment, the daily LDI test may be accomplished at the end of a flight when
the hydraulic system is at normal operating temperature.
ENGINE OPERATION
It is normal to observe high oil pressure during initial starts when the ambient temperature is 0°C or below. Run the engine
at ground idle until oil pressure is within normal operating limits (in the green range). It may take as long as 6 minutes before
pressure will return to the normal operating range. The time required for warm-up will depend on the temperature of the engine
and lubrication system before start.
During starts in extreme cold weather (below -35°C), the following oil pressure characteristics are typical:
1. Oil pressure may remain at zero for the first 15 seconds after initiating the start. Abort the start if oil pressure does not
register within 1 minute after start.
2. Once oil pressure begins to register on the gauge, it will increase rapidly and exceed the red line. Oil pressure as high
as 225 psi is possible and is normal. Oil pressure will begin to decrease shortly after reaching the peak and, depending
on the ambient temperature, may take approximately 6 minutes to fall below 100 psi (the top of the green range).
3. Oil pressure may increase above 100 psi while oil temperature is still below the normal operating range as the engine
is accelerated above ground idle. When advancing the throttle, use slower than normal rate to keep the oil pressure
within limits.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005

NORMAL PROCEDURES
MAIN GEARBOX OIL SYSTEM
After engine warm-up is complete, the main rotor may be run up to normal operating speed. Particularly when run-up
procedures include use of the rotor brake (i.e., an engine is started against the rotor brake), main gearbox oil pressure will
increase beyond the normal operating range. Oil pressure may reach as high as 115 psi in extremely cold temperatures. This
is normal. Allow the gearbox to turn with the engine at idle (observe N p /N r avoid ranges) until pressure is within normal limits.
The engine FADECs have been programmed to prevent engine acceleration if the rotor brake is on (a safety interlock). Engine
acceleration is prevented until the N p is approximately 24%. During extreme cold weather run-ups, highly viscous
transmission oil will restrict main rotor acceleration, resulting in 3 to 4 minutes delay before the N p /N r reaches 24%. If the
throttle is advanced before reaching 24% N p , the engine will not respond. Leave the throttle in ground idle until 24% N p /N r
is attained.
NOTE
During warm-up at low N , the hydraulic pumps are flow limited. It is
r
possible to have one or both TR SVO PRES cautions remain on until
pump speed is sufficient to meet pressure demand. This behavior is
acceptable. All hydraulic pressure cautions must be off by 40% N .
r
TAXIING IN SNOW
After taxiing through snow, the brakes may freeze once the aircraft is brought to a stop. If the aircraft is flown immediately,
the brakes may still be frozen upon landing. After touchdown, test that the wheels roll freely before continuing with a normal
ground taxi. If the wheels do not roll freely due to frozen brakes, hover taxi to parking.
FLIGHT IN ICING CONDITIONS
Aside from cockpit indications (caution/advisory lights, ice rate meter, etc.), a variety of visual and physical cues are available
to the pilot to indicate flight in an icing environment. The aircraft windshield wipers and associated mounting hardware
provide the pilots with an excellent visual cue to the early onset and type (rime, clear, etc.) of aircraft ice accretion. In addition,
the power required to maintain a constant flight condition will increase as the aircraft accretes ice. While operating in the
AUTO mode in some icing conditions, the aircrew may experience a gradual increase in power required of approximately
10-15% torque as the main and tail rotor blades are allowed to accrete ice during the blade heating element off-cycle. At higher
altitude and aircraft gross weight combinations the torque change associated with ice accretion/shedding may exceed these
values, which will result in reduced AEO rate of climb capability as noted in Figure 4-25. As the RIPS begins progressing
through a blade heating cycle, the main rotor system will shed ice from one set of opposing blades and then the other. For
the short period of time (approximately 5 seconds) when one blade set has shed it’s ice and the other set has not, the aircrew
may experience a slight increase in aircraft vertical 2/main rotor rev. vibrations. Because all the tail rotor blades heat at the
same time, the aircrew should not normally experience an increase in medium or high frequency airframe vibrations as the
RIPS progresses through a blade heating cycle. At the completion of the blade heating cycle, airframe vibration levels and
aircraft power requirements should return to the approximate pre-accretion values. This predictable and periodic cycling of
power requirements and aircraft vibration levels will continue for a constant icing condition (ice rate and OAT) as long as the
AUTO mode is functioning properly.
The normal/recommended operating mode for the RIPS is the AUTO mode. Either the RIPS AUTO mode or a manual mode
should be selected prior to flight into icing conditions. The engine anti-ice, Pitot heat, and windshield anti-ice should also be
on prior to entering icing conditions.
Consistently increasing or significant changes in power requirements or airframe vibration levels (i.e. not periodic) could be
an indication that the aircraft is in an environment that is outside the RIPS design envelope (freezing drizzle/rain, supercooled
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
2-36 Revised: March 4, 2011

=== DOC PAGE 109 ===
SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section II
NORMAL PROCEDURES
large drops (SLD), or conditions outside the certified envelope). Secondary indications of an encounter with freezing
drizzle/rain/SLD or other extreme icing conditions can include moisture on the windscreen, ice accretion on the cockpit
overhead windows, large/erratic fluctuations of the ice rate meter, or a full-scale deflection of the ice rate meter. The aircrew
should exit such conditions as soon as possible.
CAUTION
Flight in rotor wash from an over water hover with an OAT
less than 5°C could result in an icing condition similar to that
experienced in freezing drizzle/rain or SLD and is outside the
certified envelope of the RIPS. If the OAT is below +5°C and a
hover over water is necessary, hover height should be
increased to avoid recirculation.

HIGH WIND GROUND PROCEDURES
WARNING
The rotor blades may droop below normal levels when
starting or stopping the rotor in strong and/or gusty winds.
Ensure all equipment and personnel are clear of the rotor arc
prior to starting or stopping the rotor.
HIGH WIND ROTOR START PROCEDURE
Rotor starts have been demonstrated in winds up to 55 knots. The following procedure is recommended when starting the
aircraft in winds above 30 knots.
1. Align the aircraft with the nose into the prevailing wind.
2. Position the main rotor blades in an X configuration with the blades 45° from the axis of the aircraft.
3 Apply the rotor brake prior to engine start with at least 450 psi of brake pressure.
1
4. With the ground pump on, position the flight controls with the pedals and longitudinal cyclic centered, lateral cyclic ⁄ 2
inch right of center and collective one inch above full down.
NOTE
Avoid positioning the collective full down in high winds with the rotor
stopped. Minimum static blade flapping can be achieved with the
collective approximately two to three inches above full down.
5. Turn off the ground pump.
NOTE
Once the ground pump is turned off the collective will rise above the
preset position. This is normal.
6. Start both engines against the rotor brake.
7. Release the rotor brake.
8. Slowly lower the collective to full down when system 1 and 2 hydraulic pressure are in the green.
9. Adjust the throttles to maintain N r between 50 and 55%.

10. Advance the throttles to FLY.

Rotor stops have been demonstrated in winds up to 45 knots. The following procedure is recommended when stopping the
rotor in winds above 30 knots.
1. Align the aircraft with the nose into the prevailing wind.
2. Accomplish the required two minute engine cool down with the throttles in FLY.
3. Throttles — IDLE.
4. Position the cyclic to avoid droop stop pounding (approximately centered).
5. Center the pedals.
6. Position the collective two inches above full down.
7. Throttles — OFF.
8. Rotor brake — Apply between 40 and 25% N r .

Part 1, Section III SA S92A-RFM-006
EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
INTRODUCTION
The procedures in this section deal with common emergencies. The action taken in each emergency must relate to the complete
situation. This section does not cover compound emergencies where deviation from the normal emergency procedure may
occur.
Throughout this section, the terms 9 land immediately 9 , 9 land as soon as possible 9 and 9 land as soon as practical 9 are used to
delineate the urgency of the emergency.
Land immediately — Continued flight may not be possible. Ditching or landing in hazardous terrain is preferable to
continuing flight.
Land as soon as possible — Land at the nearest site where a safe landing can be accomplished.
Land as soon as practical — Extended flight is not recommended. Landing site and duration of flight are at the pilot’s
discretion.
Autorotate — Adjust the flight controls to establish an autorotative descent and landing.
NOTE
Many of the malfunctions described in this section are accompanied by
warnings, cautions, the master caution light, and in some cases, aural
cues in the headset. When the MSTR CAUTION light illuminates, it
should be acknowledged by pressing the light on either master warning
panel. This resets the master caution alerting function for the future. An
aural alert can be eliminated and reset for another condition by pressing
the voice cancel switch on either cyclic.
NOTE
Illumination of the MSTR CAUTION light indicates that a new
caution or warning is displayed on the EICAS page.
NOTE
Several emergency procedures require the APU to be started in flight. It
is possible to have a momentary FIRE warning light and APU FIRE
push button illuminated when starting the APU in some flight regimes.
NOTE
Different system malfunctions may cause one or more circuit breakers
to pop. A circuit breaker should be reset only if the affected system is
required for flight. The pilot should reset a circuit breaker only once and
only if there is no indication of electrical fire.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005

1.0 ENGINE FAILURE
Engine system malfunctions generally are of three types:
1. Partial or total failure of the engine to provide power.
2. Failure of an engine control system.
3. Failure of the engine auxiliary system (lubrication, torque, N g , etc).
During an engine malfunction the crew must diagnose which engine has the malfunction before any action is taken.
1.1 EMERGENCY ENGINE SHUTDOWN
If an engine malfunctions while the aircraft is on the ground, accomplish an emergency engine shutdown. An emergency
engine shutdown is also required in flight for certain engine malfunctions. To perform an emergency engine shutdown, do the
following:
Action:
1. Throttle (affected engine) — STOP.
2. FUEL (affected engine) — OFF.
If TGT remains above 540° or there is other evidence of combustion after engine shutdown:
3. ENG START button — PRESS to engage starter with throttle in STOP.
When TGT is below 150°:
4. ENG START button — PRESS to turn starter off.
1.2 ENGINE RESTART IN FLIGHT
NOTE
Engine restart may be attempted after flameout subject to the pilot’s
evaluation of the cause. The procedure that follows assumes the engine
was operating with the fuel selector in DIRECT. If the flameout
occurred while operating in XFD, place the fuel selector switch to
DIRECT during the restart sequence. The engine inlet anti-ice will not
function when the engine is not running. In icing conditions,
consideration should be given to potential engine inlet ice accretion
before restarting a failed engine in flight.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
3-3

An emergency start is only to be used when the situation dictates that damage to the engine is secondary to safety of flight.
NOTE
FADEC 5.21 includes an automatic blow down feature which will
prevent engine start until TGT decreases below 150°C when the throttle
is in IDLE. The emergency engine start procedure overrides the
automatic blow down. Returning the throttle to IDLE after engine light
off will retain hot start protection.

2.0 DUAL-ENGINE FAILURE
WARNING
N r will decay rapidly to an unrecoverable state with resultant
loss of aircraft control unless autorotation is entered im-
mediately after a dual engine failure.
NOTE
Dual engine failure requires immediate action for a power-off landing.
Varied conditions under which engine failure may occur prevent
dictating a standard procedure. Thorough knowledge of the helicopter’s
characteristics and emergency procedures will enable the pilot to
respond correctly. Altitude and airspeed where the engines fail will
dictate the action taken to ensure a safe landing. Upon dual engine
failure, the helicopter nose will swing to the left due to reduction in
torque as the engine power decreases. Immediate collective reduction is
required to maintain N r within safe limits. Full down collective should
be maintained until N r recovers to the normal operating range. Once N r
is within the normal operating range, the collective should be applied to
maintain N r within the desired limits. Rudder pedals should be applied
to maintain heading.
2.1 DUAL ENGINE FAILURE WHILE HOVERING OR ON TAKEOFF AT 10 FEET OR LESS
WARNING
Failure to move the cyclic forward while lowering the collec-
tive can decrease the main rotor blade to tail cone clearance
and increase the possibility of striking the tail cone with a
rotor blade.
Action:
1. Hold the aircraft in level attitude.
2. Increase the collective as required to cushion the landing.
After ground contact:
3. Lower collective to minimum.
4. Apply wheel brakes.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
3-10B Revised: March 4, 2011

2.3 DUAL ENGINE FAILURE DURING CRUISE
A safe autorotative landing can be accomplished if the helicopter is being flown at a safe altitude/airspeed combination and
there is sufficient terrain clearance to reach a suitable landing area. If altitude and conditions permit, an air restart should be
attempted.

80 KIAS and 100 to 105% N r . The maximum glide distance of 0.6
nm/1000 feet may be attained at 100 KIAS and 100 to 105% N r .
Action:

2. Establish autorotative glide between 80 and 100 KIAS.
3. LDG GEAR — DN.
4. Fuel and engine throttles — OFF.
5. Cabin occupants — Alert.
If time and altitude permit:
6. Try to restart one or both engines.

2.4 AUTOROTATIVE LANDINGS
NOTE
Practice touchdown autorotations are prohibited.
NOTE
When increasing collective to cushion an autorotative landing, the N r
will droop well below 96% causing the AC generators to drop off line
at touchdown. Unless the APU is on and the APU generator switch is on,
only the battery bus will be available to power aircraft systems. This
will not cause any degradation to aircraft control but will cause the
copilot MFD’s to blank.
Action:
1. Establish 80 to 100 KIAS autorotative glide. Recommended flare airspeed is 85 KIAS minimum.
2. Maintain N r at 105%.
3. LDG GEAR — DN.
4. At 100 feet, execute a flare to decrease airspeed, decrease sink rate and increase N r .
5. As the flare loses effectiveness and the helicopter starts to settle, reduce flare to a maximum 10° nose up.
6. Prior to ground contact, increase collective to cushion landing.
7. Immediately after landing decrease collective and neutralize cyclic.
8. Apply wheel brakes.

3.0 ENGINE CONTROL SYSTEM MALFUNCTIONS
NOTE
FADEC faults cannot be corrected in flight by pilot action.
3.1 ENGINE HOT START
Symptom:
ENG 1 HOT START or ENG 2 HOT START
NOTE
The FADEC hot start prevention logic should automatically abort a
normal start attempt when TGT reaches 1000°. Automatic hot start
prevention is not provided during emergency start procedures.
Confirming:
TGT is greater than 1000° during start.
Action:
1. Throttle (affected engine) — STOP.
2. ENG START button — PRESS.
3. Motor engine until TGT decreases below 250°.

Symptom:
FADEC 1A FAIL or FADEC 1B FAIL or FADEC 2A FAIL or FADEC 2B FAIL
Confirming:
Channel A Failure:
Loss of the affected engine oil temperature and TGT indications.
ENG POWER LIM caution illuminates.
ENG OIL HOT, FUEL BYPASS and ENG OIL PRES cautions are disabled.
Channel B Failure:
Loss of affected engine oil press and TGT indications.
ENG POWER LIM caution illuminates.

SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section III

Discussion:
The loss of both N p signals and the N r signal to a FADEC will cause the affected engine to remain at the power set at the time
of the sensor failures. The engine with the faulted FADEC will not respond to collective changes, while the engine with the
good FADEC will compensate for the failed system up to the limit of the engine. The procedure to be followed is dependent
upon the power setting of the failed engine.
NOTE
A FADEC malfunction may appear to be an engine failure at first
glance. An engine failure will always be accompanied by a #1 ENG
OUT or #2 ENG OUT warning light on the master warning panel, an
9 ENGINE FAILURE 9 aural alert, and a red X over the failed engine pod
on the EICAS page. An engine with a FADEC malfunction will not have
any of the associated engine failure indications and will have an N g
above 50% when airborne (above 63% when on the ground).

CAUTION
If possible, the pilot should fly the final approach and landing
using single engine landing procedures. Changes in air-
speed and altitude may cause the malfunctioning engine to
either stall or over-speed.
If an engine malfunctions at a high power setting, the pilot must ensure that the total torque demanded is more than the fixed
torque setting of the malfunctioning engine. When total torque demanded is less than the torque of the malfunctioning engine,
the rotor system will over-speed. In the event of an engine malfunctioning to a high power setting, the pilot may be required
to shut the affected engine down to prevent rotor over-speed during descent and landing.
If an engine malfunctions at a cruise power setting, the pilot should be able to accomplish a normal/shallow approach and
landing, ensuring that demanded power is never less than the torque of the malfunctioning engine. If an engine malfunctions
at a low power setting, the pilot should accomplish a single engine approach and landing procedure. Prior to reducing
collective after landing, the malfunctioning engine should be shut down to prevent over-speeding the rotor system.
WARNING
In a ( fail fixed ( condition, there is no automatic engine
overspeed protection.
Action:
1. Airspeed — 80 KIAS.
2. Collective — Make small changes to confirm 9 fail fixed 9 condition.
NOTE
During a 9 fail fixed 9 condition, the affected engine torque will remain
constant while the good engine torque will vary to maintain a constant
dual engine power setting.
3. Collective — Reduce until a rate of descent is obtained or N r increases above 106%.
NOTE
If a descent rate can be obtained at 80 KIAS then the subsequent
approach and landing may be made with the 9 fail fixed 9 engine on line.
If N r increases above 106% and torque on the good engine reaches 0 before a rate of descent can be established:
4. Throttle (affected engine) — STOP.

3.13 ENGINE COMPRESSOR STALL
Symptom:
Bang or popping noise and possible aircraft yaw kicks.
Confirming:
Rapid increase in TGT.
Decrease in Torque.
Fluctuations in N g and N p .
WARNING
Flight through extreme air temperature environments, such
as in close proximity to intense fires, volcanic activity or over
smoke or fire stacks, may cause rapid engine inlet air
temperature changes and increases the probability of
compressor stalls on one or both engines. This may exceed
engine limitations causing damage to engine components
and, in extreme cases, can also increase the probability of
engine power loss or engine shutdown.

3. Throttle (affected engine) — FLY.

4. Obtain safe single engine airspeed.

6. Accomplish SINGLE ENGINE FAILURE procedure.

NOTE
The fuel prime pump supplies pressurized fuel during engine starts
when the fuel valve is selected to the direct (DIR) position. When starts
are made in the crossfeed (XFD) position, the prime fuel is sent to the
opposite engine. When starting the second engine with the fuel valves in

7.0 GEAR BOX MALFUNCTIONS
The main gearbox temperature and pressure gauges, along with the main gearbox chip detection system, provide the pilot with
information to diagnose and take corrective action in the event of a main gearbox malfunction. An input module chip
indication requires retarding the affected engine to IDLE to remove power from that module. Indications of low oil pressure
or high oil temperature dictate that the helicopter should land as soon as possible. An imminent transmission failure would
necessitate that the helicopter land immediately.
After presentation of an MGB oil pressure warning or caution, any one of the following symptoms are indicative of an
imminent transmission failure: MGB oil pressure below 5 psi, an increase in power required to maintain a constant collective
setting and airspeed, yaw kicks, loss of two hydraulic pumps, or unusual noise or vibrations.
If an imminent failure is suspected, the primary consideration is to land the aircraft before the failure progresses to a gearbox
seizure or loss of drive to the main or tail rotor. The descent should be made at a reduced power setting but with at least 15%
torque to ensure the engines continue to drive the transmission. Avoid rapid or frequent power changes. A running landing is
preferred since it requires less power and smaller power changes. A no-hover landing should be performed if a running landing
area is not available.
Low MGB oil pressure can be caused by an oil leak or a pump failure. Oil leaks can occur either in the gearbox housings or
the external cooler. Different scenarios are discussed below.
The MGB bypass system is designed to contain leaks in the external cooler. If the MGB bypass switch is activated in time
to capture sufficient oil to allow continued flight, MGB pressure should stabilize above 5 psi and MGB temperature will
increase into the red zone. As the MGB oil pressure stabilizes, the switch should be left in the BYP position. An inadvertent
activation of the BYP switch will not harm the MGB if the switch is returned to the NORM position before oil temperature
exceeds limits. Do not come out of bypass if the MGB OIL PRES warning is illuminated.
Oil leaks in the gearbox housings will not be contained by the bypass system and can lead to a rapid total loss of lubrication
oil. The red MGB OIL PRES warning light, coupled with pressure below 5 psi may be the only indications of total oil loss.
WARNING
A total loss of MGB oil pressure may result in MGB failure in
less than 10 minutes. If MGB OIL PRES is less than 5 psi,
Land Immediately.
A pump failure will lead to low oil pressure which will fluctuate between 5 to 25 psi and may result in high temperatures in
the corresponding accessory and input modules (indicated by an INPUT 1/2 CHIP caution). If possible, the pilot should
retard the engine on the affected side to IDLE to reduce heating due to churning oil.
CAUTION
High oil temperatures or loss of lubrication may result in loss
of the main generators. The APU should be started so that the
APU generator will be immediately available.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
Revised: May 13, 2009

10.0 LANDING GEAR
Normal landing gear extension is indicated by illumination of the three green lights without the red UNLKD light illuminated
on the landing gear panel. Any other combination of lights may indicate a gear malfunction or the possibility of a burned out
indicator bulb.
After experiencing a landing gear malfunction, if a safe landing gear indication is obtained (three green lights and no red light),
do not cycle the gear. If the landing gear cannot be extended safely, landing on a cradle or some other fixture should be
accomplished.
CAUTION
With asymmetrical landing gear extension, the aircraft could
roll over. Consideration should be given to evacuating all
nonessential crew and passengers in a ( light on wheels
hover ( before putting the full weight of the aircraft on the
landing gear.

11.0 TAIL ROTOR MALFUNCTIONS
Tail rotor malfunctions may be caused by a wide variety of mechanical failures with an equally broad range of resultant
severity. It is imperative that the fight crew recognize the differences in the symptoms associated with each failure mode and
to also recognize an impending failure.
Tail rotor malfunctions may be classified into two major categories:
Loss of tail rotor thrust.
Loss of tail rotor control.
With loss of tail rotor thrust, it is impossible to remain in level flight. This failure is associated with a loss in drive and
characterized by a sharp, right yaw of the aircraft that requires immediate entry into autorotation (if in forward flight) or
landing (if in a hover). If thrust is lost in forward flight (60 KIAS or above) roll excursions up to 10°, pitch attitude changes
up to 5° and heading changes up to 50° may be experienced during the transition to autorotation. Once established in
autorotation the aircraft can be flown to a stable pitch and roll attitude with an acceptable level of sideslip.
Loss of tail rotor control is the inability to change tail rotor blade pitch because of a mechanical failure in the yaw flight control
path, either due to a mechanical restriction or the loss of both tail rotor control cables. The tail rotor is still producing thrust
however, and is less critical than a loss of drive. With a bind or restriction, the pilot must deal with a tail rotor stuck at 9 fixed
pitch 9 ; the amount of which is dependent upon the rudder pedal position when the failure takes place.
Hardovers may initially present the appearance of a loss of control but are generally easier to respond to and isolate because
of the ability to turn off the runaway actuator. See the procedures for SAS HARDOVERS, BOOST HARDOVERS and
TRIM HARDOVERS.
Impending tail rotor drive failure may be preceded by excessive noise or vibration from the tail rotor section, often felt by the
pilot as a middle frequency 9 buzz 9 through the rudder pedals.
11.1 LOSS OF TAIL ROTOR THRUST IN FORWARD FLIGHT
Symptoms:
Uncommanded sharp right yaw, unresponsive to pedal inputs.
Action:
1. Enter autorotation.
2. Maintain 80 to 100 KIAS.
3. LDG GEAR — DOWN.
4. Throttles — STOP prior to touchdown.
11.2 LOSS OF TAIL ROTOR THRUST IN A HOVER
Symptoms:
Uncommanded sharp right yaw/spin, unresponsive to pedal inputs.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
3-51

Action:
1. Hold the aircraft in level attitude, attempt to achieve zero groundspeed and drift in a low hover.
2. Throttles — STOP (5 to 10 feet).
3. Collective — Increase to cushion landing.
After ground contact:
4. Lower collective to minimum.
5. Apply wheel brakes.
11.3 TAIL ROTOR CABLE FAILURE
Loss of one or both tail rotor cables will be indicated by illumination of the TR QUAD caution capsule. If only one cable
fails, no change in handling qualities should occur. If both cables fail, a centering spring will position the tail rotor servo
linkage to provide a preset amount of pitch. This will allow trimmed flight at about 30 KIAS and 150 KIAS (these speeds will
vary with gross weight). At airspeeds below 30 and above 150 KIAS, right yaw can be controlled by reducing collective.
Between 30 and 150 KIAS, left yaw can be controlled by increasing collective.
During the approach, a yaw to the left will occur. As the touchdown point is approached, a mild deceleration should be
executed to reduce airspeed. As collective is increased to cushion touchdown, the nose of the helicopter will yaw right. Careful
adjustment of collective and deceleration should allow touchdown with approximate runway alignment. After landing, lower
collective carefully. Use brakes to control heading.
Symptom:
TR QUAD
Action:
1. Push either tail rotor pedal.
If normal yaw control is observed:
2. Land as soon as practical.
If the aircraft does not respond to pedal inputs:
3. Adjust airspeed to reduce yaw.
4. Perform a shallow approach to a roll on landing.
5. Lower collective slowly.
6. Use differential braking to control heading.

12.0 AUTOMATIC FLIGHT CONTROL SYSTEM
One or more system failures may cause Automatic Flight Control System (AFCS) malfunctions. The pilot should observe
aircraft attitude changes and EICAS cautions to determine the appropriate procedure to follow after an AFCS malfunction.
SAS hardovers will cause abrupt, uncommanded aircraft attitude changes in one or more axes without a corresponding
pilot’s flight control movement.
Boost hardovers will cause rapid, uncommanded flight control movements in one axis with a corresponding change in
aircraft attitude.
Trim hardovers will cause slow, uncommanded aircraft attitude changes in one or more axes with a corresponding flight
control movement.
The AFCS control panel lights should only be used to determine which systems have been selected.
The TRIM, SAS and PRI/SEC lights on the AFCS control panel show switch position only. Illumination of these lights
indicates that function is selected but does not ensure that function is operational. If electrical power is interrupted, these
lights will remain illuminated.
When the AP lights on the AFCS control panel are lit, the system is selected and powered. If electrical power is interrupted
to the AP system, the AP lights will go blank.
12.1 AUTOPILOT FAIL
The following conditions can result in an autopilot fail caution: cyclic trim fault, yaw trim fault, attitude/heading hold not
available, attitude hold fault and heading hold fault.
Symptom:
AUTOPILOT 1 FAIL and/or AUTOPILOT 2 FAIL
CAUTION
Failure of the Weight On Wheels (WOW) system may result in
the failure of the landing gear to retract, AFCS #1 and #2 ATT
mode not engaging, and the transponder, weather radar and
TCAS remaining in the standby mode. Although not indicated
in the cockpit, such a WOW failure would also prohibit the
RIPS from heating the main and tail rotor blades. If any of
these secondary symptoms of a WOW failure exist, avoid
flight in icing conditions.
Action:
If accompanied by uncommanded aircraft attitude changes, follow the appropriate TRIM or SAS HARDOVER
procedure.
Otherwise:

12.5 SAS HARDOVERS
Symptom:
Abrupt, uncommanded aircraft attitude change in one or more axes without a corresponding pilot’s flight control
movement.
Confirming:
PSAS 1 FAULT or PSAS 2 FAULT or AFCS DGRD or FD DGRD or AUTOPILOT 1 FAIL or AUTOPILOT
2 FAIL may or may not accompany SAS hardovers.
Action:
1. Adjust flight controls to maintain aircraft control.
2. Reduce airspeed to 120 KIAS or less.
3. Disable the malfunctioning system by pressing the appropriate SAS button.
4. Continue the flight while actively monitoring the controls.
12.6 BOOST HARDOVERS
Symptom:
Rapid, uncommanded flight control movement in one axis with corresponding change in aircraft attitude, if airborne.
Confirming:
AFCS DGRD or FD DGRD may or may not accompany boost hardovers.
Action:
1. Adjust flight controls to maintain aircraft control.
2. SERVO BST — OFF.
3. If airborne, reduce airspeed to 120 KIAS or less.
4. Land as soon as practical.
12.7 TRIM HARDOVERS
Symptom:
Slow, uncommanded aircraft attitude change in one or more axes with a corresponding flight control movement.

Temporary Revisions
TEMPORARY REVISION NO. 7
FILING INSTRUCTIONS: Insert this temporary revision facing page 3-59, dated July 17, 2007.
SUBJECT: JAMMED OR RESTRICTED FLIGHT CONTROLS. This temporary revision adds a Jammed or
Restricted Flight Controls procedure to the Automatic Flight Control System section of the Emergency
procedures.
MANUAL CHANGES: Insert the following procedure between the procedures labeled 12.7 TRIM HARDOVERS
and 12.8 FLIGHT DIRECTOR ALTITUDE DEGRADED.
12.7A JAMMED OR RESTRICTED FLIGHT CONTROLS
Symptom:
Bind or restriction in cyclic or collective.
Confirming:
AFCS DGRD or FD DGRD or AUTOPILOT 1 FAIL or AUTOPILOT 2 FAIL may or may not accompany
jammed or restricted flight controls.
Action:
NOTE
Trim actuators incorporate a slip clutch that provides an override capability in the
event of a jammed trim actuator. The pilot applied forces required to overcome
the slip clutch are approximately 15 pounds in pitch, 12 pounds in roll and 30
pounds in collective.
1. Adjust flight controls to maintain aircraft control.
2. Reduce airspeed to 120 KIAS or less.
3. Check for foreign objects in the cockpit impeding the flight controls.
4. Trim – OFF (affected control).
If control continues to be restricted:
5. Trim – ON (affected control).
If control continues to be restricted:
6. SERVO BST – OFF.
If control continues to be restricted:
7. SERVO BST – ON.
If control continues to be restricted:
8. If possible, manually apply sufficient force to overcome restriction.
9. Land as soon as possible.

NOTE
The SAS system will initially counteract a trim hardover resulting in a

NOTE
Following a cyclic trim failure, the pilot should still push and release the
cyclic trim release button when established at a desired airspeed. This
action will enhance airspeed stability.
12.8 FLIGHT DIRECTOR ALTITUDE DEGRADED
Certain system malfunctions will prevent the flight management system (FMS) and flight control computers (FCC) from
receiving the correct altimeter setting. This may degrade the accuracy and performance of the flight director altitude hold and
FMS vertical navigation functions.
Symptoms:
FD 1 ALT DGRD or FD 2 ALT DGRD
Action:
1. Continue the flight using the non-degraded flight director.
If both cautions are illuminated or ADC reversion is selected:
2. Continue the flight without using the flight director altitude or FMS vertical navigation functions.

4. Both throttles — OFF.
5. Rotor Brake — Apply.
6. BATT and APU CTRL — OFF.
7. Evacuate aircraft.
In flight:
1. Confirm fire.
2. Collective — Adjust to single engine power.

=== DOC PAGE 188 ===
Part 1, Section III SA S92A-RFM-006
EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
NOTE
DCU MISCOMPARE is an indication that data from the two DCUs do
not agree and is usually caused by differences between external sensors.
Complete failure of one DCU will also illuminate the DCU
MISCOMPARE caution and the appropriate DCU fail indication. The
pilot can also differentiate between a simple miscompare and a DCU
failure by checking an EICAS page on both sides of the cockpit. A
simple miscompare will still present full data on both EICAS pages, and
may display dual-headed arrows on the discrepant parameters. In the
event of a DCU failure, the failed side EICAS page will have no data.
Action:
In flight:
1. Select an EICAS page on both sides of the cockpit.
2. Determine if the condition is a simple miscompare or a DCU failure.
If the condition is a simple DCU miscompare:
3. Continue the flight.
If the condition is a DCU failure:
4. Determine which DCU has failed.
5. REVERSION CONTROL DCU — Select good system.
6. AFCS CONTROL PANEL — Select the FD that corresponds to the good DCU.
NOTE
After a single DCU failure, select the FD that corresponds to the
functioning DCU to ensure power limiting is available during coupled
flight.
7. Continue the flight in VMC.
If VMC is not available:
8. Land as soon as practical.
On the ground:
1. Do not conduct flight in IMC until fault is corrected.

14.7 DUAL DCU FAILURE
NOTE
If both DCUs fail, the performance of the aircraft will not be affected
but the pilot will not be able to monitor aircraft health. Most cautions
and warnings will not be available. Most aural alerts will not be
available. Attitude, heading, airspeed, and altitude displays will be
available. Navigation and communication radios and displays will be
available. Full AFCS functionality will be available.
Symptom:
DCU 1 and DCU 2
No data presented on either side EICAS display.
No N r , N p , TGT or Q data on either PFD.
Action:
1. Land as soon as possible.

Normal HUMS system monitoring will not be available after a
maintenance computer failure. The pilot shall record any engine or
gearbox exceedances that occur during the time flown with an inopera-
tive maintenance computer and report these exceedances to
maintenance.

15.5 RIPS RIPS FAILURE
Symptom:
DEICE SYS FAIL
ICE icon appears on both PFDs
NOTE
If an inboard MFD is turned off or fails, the same side RIPS controller
will not function until the MFD is rebooted. If functional, the other RIPS
controller will provide RIPS control.
Discussion:
The RIPS can no longer deice the main and tail rotors. Resetting the RIPS controllers may restore system operation.
Action:
1. BLADE DEICE #1 and #2 RESET switches — Press and hold for approximately 3 seconds.
NOTE
Resetting the RIPS controllers will temporarily remove power from the
system. The reset process can take from 30 to 90 seconds, during which
time the RIPS will not be deicing the rotor system. If flying in icing
conditions during a controller reset, the rotor system will continue to
accrete ice during the reset process.
If normal RIPS function is restored:
2. Continue flight in icing conditions at pilot’s discretion.

If normal RIPS function is not restored:

15.6 RIPS RIPS MAIN ROTOR FAULT
Symptom:
MR DEICE FAULT
Discussion:
One of the heating zones on the main rotor is malfunctioning which may lead to abnormal/asymmetric ice accretion/shedding.
Asymmetric ice accretion or shedding may result in an unbalanced main rotor condition and increased main rotor vibrations.
Main rotor ice accretion may also lead to increased power requirements.
Action:
1. BLADE DEICE #1 and #2 RESET switches — Press and hold for approximately 3 seconds.
NOTE
Resetting the RIPS controllers will temporarily remove power from the
system. The reset process can take from 30 to 90 seconds, during which
time the RIPS will not be deicing the rotor system. If flying in icing
conditions during a controller reset, the rotor system will continue to
accrete ice during the reset process.
If normal RIPS function is restored:
2. Continue flight.
If normal RIPS function is not restored:
3. Monitor aircraft vibrations and power requirements.
If aircraft vibrations or power requirements increase significantly:
4. Exit icing conditions.
5. Avoid further flight in icing conditions.

15.8 RIPS RIPS AUTO MODE FAILURE
Symptom:
AUTO DEICE FAIL
Discussion:
Although the RIPS automatic mode has failed, the manual modes may still function properly. The pilot should use visual cues
of ice accretion or the ice rate displayed prior to the system failure to judge the proper manual mode for the existing conditions.
CAUTION
Selection of the improper manual mode can lead to excessive
ice accretion (if the blades are not heated frequently enough)
or run-back ice (if the blades are heated too frequently).
Run-back ice occurs when water from melted ice flows to an
unprotected part of the blade and refreezes.
Action:
1. BLADE DEICE #1 and #2 RESET switches — Press and hold for approximately 3 seconds.
NOTE
Resetting the RIPS controllers will temporarily remove power from the
system. The reset process can take from 30 to 90 seconds, during which
time the RIPS will not be deicing the rotor system. If flying in icing
conditions during a controller reset, the rotor system will continue to
accrete ice during the reset process.
If normal RIPS function is restored:
2. Continue flight.
If normal RIPS function is not restored:
3. Select appropriate manual RIPS mode.

Revised: July 17, 2007

NOTE
During normal system operation, aircraft vibrations (a vertical 2/main
rotor revolution vibration under some conditions) and power require-

may cycle as the rotor blades accrete and shed ice. At higher altitude and
aircraft gross weight combinations, the torque change associated with
ice accretion/shedding may exceed these values, which will result in

power requirements that peak higher than normal while in a manual
mode may indicate that the next highest manual mode is more
appropriate for the existing icing conditions. Steadily increasing as
opposed to cyclical vibration levels and power requirements may be an
indication of run-back ice.

15.12 RIPS DUAL RIPS LIQUID WATER CONTENT (LWC) SENSOR FAILURE
Symptoms:
RIPS DGRD LWC
Both ice rate meters disappear.
Discussion:
The RIPS will continue to sense OAT to schedule blade heating element on time. However, without LWC input, the RIPS
AUTO mode will schedule blade heating element off time based on a default LWC. The default LWC value is equivalent to
a mid LIGHT icing level. If placed in a manual mode, the RIPS will schedule blade heating element off time based on the
LWC associated with that particular manual mode and will continue to schedule blade heating element on time based on actual
OAT.
CAUTION
A significant difference between the actual cloud LWC and
the RIPS default LWC can lead to excessive ice accretion (if
the blades are not heated frequently enough) or run-back ice
(if the blades are heated too frequently). Run-back ice occurs
when water from melted ice flows to an unprotected part of
the blade and refreezes.
Action:
1. Monitor aircraft vibrations and power requirements.
If aircraft vibrations or power requirements increase significantly:
2. Select appropriate manual RIPS mode based on visual indications of ice accretion or the system displayed ice rate prior
to the failure.
NOTE
During normal system operation, aircraft vibrations (a vertical 2/main
rotor revolution vibration under some conditions) and power require-
ments (up to approximately 15% torque change under some conditions)
may cycle as the rotor blades accrete and shed ice. At higher altitude and
aircraft gross weight combinations the torque change associated with ice
accretion/shedding may exceed these values, which will result in
reduced AEO rate of climb capability as noted in Figure 4-25. Steadily
increasing as opposed to cyclical vibration levels and power require-
ments may be an indication of run-back ice.
If aircraft vibrations or power requirements continue to steadily increase:
3. Exit icing conditions.

17.0 FLOAT DITCHING
The flotation system is designed only for emergency landing on water and is expected to keep the helicopter upright long
enough to permit passengers and crew to exit to life rafts or rescue boats. A subsequent takeoff or long term towing should
not be attempted.
When it appears that ditching is likely, consideration must be given to such factors as wind direction and velocity, sea state
conditions and helicopter power available for ditching. Optimum ditching conditions would occur in a calm sea state with near
zero forward and lateral helicopter speed. Minimum touchdown forces will be achieved when touchdown is made on the crest
or back of a wave with a minimum rate of descent. Greatly increased touchdown forces will be experienced if the landing is
made on the front or rising face of a wave. Every effort should be made to land the helicopter with as little sideward drift as
possible as the roll rate after touchdown increases sharply with any increase in lateral motion. Ditching with power available
(such as when fuel starvation is imminent, or a loss of transmission oil pressure dictates such action) will greatly increase
controllability, reduce touchdown forces, and assist in preventing the helicopter from rolling after impact. Power off ditching
(autorotation) should be avoided if possible. The floats are not designed to absorb the force of water impact and must only
be deployed after water entry. When the flotation system is armed, the floats will automatically deploy via the immersion
switch or manually deploy via the collective mounted FLOAT switch. The pilot should manually deploy the floats immediately
after water entry.
NOTE
Automatic float deployment will not function when operating on battery
power only. Manual float deployment will function when operating on
battery power.
NOTE
At aircraft weights at or above 18,590 pounds (8,432 kilograms), the
three float flotation system is certified for ditching in conditions up to
and including sea state 5.
NOTE
At aircraft weights at or above 18,590 pounds (8,432 kilograms), the
five float flotation system is certified for ditching in conditions up to and
including sea state 6.
NOTE
At aircraft weights below 18,590 pounds (8,432 kilograms), both
flotation systems are certified for ditching in conditions up to and
including sea state 4.
Action:
1. LDG GEAR — DOWN.
NOTE
If the landing gear cannot be extended for any reason, the floats can be
deployed with the gear retracted.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
3-82 Revised: May 2, 2012

18.0 FLOAT FLOATS AND RAFT MALFUNCTIONS
18.1 FLOAT INADVERTENT FLOTATION DEPLOYMENT
Intentional in-flight deployment of the float bags is prohibited. The following procedures should be followed in the event of
an inadvertent float bag deployment.
Symptom:
Noticeable bang followed by float bags appearing outside the pilot and copilot windows.
Action:
1. Restrict rate of climb to 1000 fpm or less.
2. Restrict angle of bank to 30° or less.
3. Adhere to the float deployed airspeed restrictions as shown below.
NOTE
Deployed floats will adversely affect the accuracy of the airspeed
system. The indicated airspeeds shown below will produce an 80 knot
calibrated airspeed.
Maximum Indicated Airspeed with Floats Deployed
Flight Condition Maximum Indicated Airspeed
Climb 50
Level Flight 55
Descent/Autorotation 60
4. Land as soon as practical.
CAUTION
Restrict flare attitude on landing touchdown to 8° or less to
avoid hitting the aft float bag.
CAUTION
Due to decreased airspeed and increased drag, aircraft range
will be severely limited with floats deployed.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005

PERFORMANCE INFORMATION
PART 1, SECTION IV
PERFORMANCE INFORMATION
GENERAL
ENGINE HEALTH
The performance charts are predicated on engines that deliver specification power. No performance credit is to be taken for
above specification power (i.e., positive power margin).
CROSSWIND LIMITS
Category 9 A 9 horizontal takeoffs and landings are limited to 35 knots of crosswind component or less.
Category 9 A 9 ground level helipad takeoffs and landings are limited to 22 knots of crosswind component or less.
WIND ACCOUNTABILITY
Several charts in this section provide performance credit for 9 unfactored headwinds. 9 The data from these charts reflects the
actual performance in the presence of headwinds. Unless otherwise authorized by operating regulations, the pilot is not
authorized to credit more than 50 percent of the performance increase resulting from the actual headwind component and must
reduce performance by 150 percent of the performance decrement resulting from the actual tail wind component.
CATEGORY ( A ( HORIZONTAL TAKEOFF DISTANCE
The Category 9 A 9 horizontal takeoff procedure shown diagrammatically in Figure 4-7 features variable Takeoff Decision
Points (TDP) and Takeoff Safety Speeds (V toss ). The TDP, expressed only in terms of airspeed, is selectable in 1 knot
increments between 30 and 48 knots. V toss is TDP + 15 knots. This permits payload to be traded off against available field
length in such a manner that Category 9 A 9 one engine inoperative (OEI) climb performance minima can be maintained over
a wide range of environmental conditions.
Figure 4-8 shows the Rejected Takeoff (RTO) and Continued Takeoff (CTO) distances as a function of pressure altitude,
temperature, TDP speed, and headwind component. RTO and CTO distances are directly proportional to TDP speed, therefore
lower TDP speeds equate to shorter field lengths. Figure 4-9 shows the maximum takeoff and landing gross weight as a
function of pressure altitude, temperature, and TDP speed. Maximum takeoff and landing gross weight is also directly
proportional to TDP speed, therefore higher TDP speeds equate to higher maximum takeoff gross weights.
The Category 9 A 9 takeoff procedure provides the flexibility to address specific payload and/or field length requirements
appropriate to either of the following operational scenarios:
v Determine the maximum takeoff gross weight, given the available field length.
v Determine the required field length, given the desired mission takeoff gross weight.
CATEGORY ( A ( HORIZONTAL LANDING DISTANCE
See Figure 4-15 for Category 9 A 9 landing distance.
CATEGORY ( A ( VERTICAL GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD
The Category 9 A 9 vertical ground level helipad takeoff profile is shown in Figure 4-16.

Maximum gross weight for a Category 9 A 9 vertical takeoff can be found in Figure 4-17. When departing over obstacles, a
higher TDP may be required. The bottom portion of Figure 4-17 estimates the decrease in maximum allowable gross weight
due to a higher TDP.
NOTE
Relatively low obstacles that are close to the helipad do not conflict with
the departure profile. See Figure 4-19 to determine the height and
position of those obstacles that can be ignored when determining the
TDP.
The maximum and minimum TDP and minimum field length can be found in Figure 4-18. The figure provides two TDP
heights. The 9 maximum reject TDP 9 is the highest height from which a rejected landing can be accomplished without damage
to the aircraft. The 9 minimum fly away TDP 9 is the lowest height from which the fly away maneuver can be accomplished
with 15 feet of clearance from the helipad altitude. When departing over obstacles, the pilot should add the height of the
obstacle to the minimum TDP. The take off field length is the horizontal distance (measured from the helipad) required to reach
35 feet above the helipad or obstacle altitude at a V toss climb, with 2 minute power selected, after an engine failure at the
minimum TDP.
CAUTION
If the minimum fly away TDP is greater than the maximum
reject TDP, safe continued flight or landing is not assured if
an engine should fail when climbing between the two TDPs.
The Category 9 A 9 ground level helipad landing profile is shown in Figure 4-20.
Maximum gross weight for a Category 9 A 9 ground level helipad landing can be found in Figure 4-21.
Figure 4-22 provides the information required to determine the Landing Decision Point (LDP) based on obstacle height and
distance of obstacles from the departure end of the helipad. All heights are referenced to the elevation of the helipad. The LDP
is the minimum height from which a balked landing can be initiated to achieve obstacle or ground clearance. The 9 balked
landing distance 9 is the horizontal distance (measured from the helipad) required to reach 45 feet above the helipad or 35 feet
above the obstacle (whichever is higher) at a V climb after an engine failure at the LDP. The 9 minimum height at balked
toss
landing distance 9 is the minimum height above the helipad level when the aircraft is in a 55 KIAS climb with 2 minute power
selected.
The balked landing path is the area on the departure side of the helipad equal to the 9 balked landing distance. 9 If there are no
obstacles over 10 feet in the balked landing path, the pilot can choose the minimum LDP of 125 feet. This will provide 25
feet of clearance above the helipad level (15 feet clearance of a 10 foot obstacle). If there are obstacles over 10 feet in the
balked landing path, enter Figure 4-22 with obstacle height to determine the minimum LDP to ensure 15 feet obstacle
clearance.
When the approach to landing is flown at 35 KIAS with a 500 FPM descent, the approach angle is approximately 8.1°. A
headwind will increase the approach angle. A faster approach speed or slower descent rate will decrease the approach angle.

SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section IV
PERFORMANCE INFORMATION
FIGURE 4-17: CATEGORY ( A ( GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD MAXIMUM TAKEOFF GROSS WEIGHT
EXAMPLES
EXAMPLE 1:
Actual aircraft weight = 24,000 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 20°C
Wind speed = 0
No obstacles in takeoff path
1. Enter the chart on the left with 0 pressure altitude.
2. Go right to the 20° temperature line.
3. Go down to 25,000 LB.
4. Since the maximum allowable gross weight is 24,500 LB, in this case, 24,500 LB will also be the maximum
takeoff weight .
5. The actual aircraft gross weight is less than the maximum takeoff weight. No need to download fuel or passengers.
6. Continue to Figure 4-18.
EXAMPLE 2:
Actual aircraft weight = 24,000 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 20°C
Wind speed = 20 knots direct headwind
50 foot obstacle 75 feet from the nose wheel
1. Enter the chart on left with 0 pressure altitude.
2. Go right to the 20° temperature line.
3. Go down past 25,000 LB to the smaller chart.
4. Follow the influence line down and left to the 50 foot obstacle line.
5. Go down to read 24,200 LB estimated maximum gross takeoff weight to clear a 50 foot obstacle.
6. The actual aircraft gross weight is less than the estimated maximum takeoff weight.
7. Continue to Figures 4-18 and 4-19 to ensure capability to clear a 50 foot obstacle at this weight.
EXAMPLE 3:
Actual aircraft weight = 23,640 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 30°C
Wind speed = 0
20 foot obstacle 50 feet from the nose wheel
1. Enter the chart on left with 0 pressure altitude.
2. Go right to the 30° temperature line.
3. Go down past 23,640 LB (0 ft obstacle maximum gross weight) to the smaller chart.
4. Follow the influence line down and left to the 20 foot obstacle line.
5. Go down to read 23,360 LB estimated maximum gross takeoff weight to clear a 20 foot obstacle.
6. Continue to Figure 4-18 using the actual aircraft weight when determining the TDP and field length, assuming
that the relatively low obstacle close to the pad may be ignored for TDP calculation in Figure 4-19.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
Revised: July 26, 2012
