FIGURE 4-18: CATEGORY ( A ( GROUND LEVEL HELIPAD TDP, V toss AND TAKEOFF DISTANCE
DETERMINATION EXAMPLES
NOTE
Due to the limitations of printed charts, there are cases in which the maximum
reject TDP may be up to 10 feet lower than the minimum fly-away TDP when
using the maximum takeoff weight from Figure 4-17. In this instance, it is
permissible to use the Figure 4-17 maximum takeoff weight and the minimum
fly-away TDP.
EXAMPLE 1:
Actual aircraft weight = 24,000 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 20°C
Wind speed = 0
No obstacles in takeoff path
1. Enter chart at top left with 0 pressure altitude.
2. Go down to the upper 20° temperature line.
3. Go right to intersect the 24,000 LB gross weight line (actual aircraft gross weight).
4. Read V toss = 40 KTS from the angular line.
5. Reenter chart at top left with 0 pressure altitude.
6. Go down to the lower 20° temperature line.
7. Go right to the 40 KTS V toss (from step 4).
8. Go down to the 0 wind line.
9. Go left for minimum fly-away TDP = 85 feet .
10. Go right for takeoff distance = 1,270 feet .
NOTE
Since this example does not include an obstacle, there is no need to use Figure
4-19.
Continue with the bottom left portion of the chart to determine maximum TDP:
11. Enter chart at bottom right with 20° temperature.
12. Go up to the 0 pressure altitude line.
13. Go left to the 24,000 LB gross weight line (actual aircraft gross weight).
14. Go up to the 20° temperature line.
15. Go right to read maximum reject TDP = 148 feet.
EXAMPLE 2:
Actual aircraft weight = 24,000 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 20°C
Wind speed = 20 knots direct headwind
50 foot obstacle 75 feet from the nose wheel
1. Follow steps 1 through 7 in example 1 above to determine takeoff distance.
2. Go down to the 10 knot wind line (50% of the 20 knot head wind).
3. Go right to read takeoff distance = 1,100 feet .
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
4-30 Revised: July 26, 2012

4. Follow steps 1 through 9 in example 1 to determine minimum fly-away TDP without an obstacle = 85 feet.
5. Continue to Figure 4-19.
Example 2 maximum reject TDP calculations are identical to example 1.
EXAMPLE 3:
Actual aircraft weight = 23,640 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 30°C
Wind speed = 0
20 foot obstacle 50 feet from the nose wheel
1. Enter chart at top left with 0 pressure altitude.
2. Go down to the upper 30° temperature line.

toss

toss

10. Since 23,640 LB gross weight is the maximum capability from Figure 4-17 with no obstacle clearance capability,
minimum fly-away TDP = maximum reject TDP , and there is no need to calculate maximum reject TDP from the
bottom portion of the chart.
11. Continue to Figure 4-19.

TAKEOFF EXAMPLES
EXAMPLE 2:
Actual aircraft weight = 24,000 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 20°C
Wind speed = 20 knots direct headwind
50 foot obstacle 75 feet from the nose wheel
1. Determine the point on the chart defined by the obstacle height (50 feet) and obstacle distance from nose wheel
(75 feet).
2. Since the point is above the minimum fly-away TDP (85 feet from Figure 4-18), you must add the 50 foot obstacle
to the 9 no obstacle 9 TDP.
3. Minimum fly-away TDP is 85 feet + 50 feet = 135 feet .
EXAMPLE 3:
Actual aircraft weight = 23,640 LB
Pressure altitude = 0
OAT = 30°C
Wind speed = 0
20 foot obstacle 50 feet from the nose wheel
1. Determine the point on the chart defined by the obstacle height (20 feet) and obstacle distance from nose wheel
(50 feet).
2. Since the point is below the minimum fly-away TDP (123 feet from Figure 4-18), Figure 4-19 allows you to
disregard the obstacle for minimum TDP calculations and there is no need to add the obstacle to the 9 no obstacle 9
TDP or to the maximum takeoff weight calculation.
3. Minimum fly-away TDP = 123 feet and maximum takeoff weight = 23,640 LB .

NOTE
Determine the intersection of the obstacle height and the obstacle distance. If
the intersection is less than or equal to the minimum fly-away TDP (from

height to the minimum fly-away TDP from Figure 4-18. If the corrected

Category 9 A 9 takeoff cannot be performed for the planned weight, altitude and
temperature with the proposed obstacle.

SA S92A-RFM-006 Part 1, Section IV
PERFORMANCE INFORMATION
NOISE LEVEL CERTIFICATION
The S-92A Aircraft is certified at gross weights up to and including 26,500 lbs. in accordance with the rules and procedures
for a Stage 2 aircraft of FAR Part 36, Subpart H.
The following noise levels comply with FAR Part 36, Subpart H, Stage 2 noise level requirements. They were obtained by
analysis of approved data from noise tests conducted under the provisions of FAR Part 36, Amendment 36-24. The test and
analysis procedures used to obtain these noise levels are equivalent to those required by the International Civil Aviation
Organization (ICAO) in Annex 16, Volume I, Chapter 8.
ICAO Annex 16, Volume I, Chapter 8 approval is applicable only after endorsement by the Civil Aviation Authority of the
country of aircraft registration.
The certified noise levels are:
EPNL (EPN dB) FLIGHT CONDITION
94.5 Takeoff
97.5 Approach
97.2 Flyover
The Flyover noise certification level is based on the S-92A noise certification V of 150.5 knots true airspeed.
H
NOTE
No determination has been made by the Federal Aviation Administration
that the noise levels of this aircraft are or should be acceptable or
unacceptable for operation at, into, or out of any airport.
FAA APPROVED: NOVEMBER 8, 2005
Revised: July 26, 2012

Cargo Ramp and Cargo Upper Door The cargo upper door has interior and exterior manually-
operated handles. Pressing the pushbutton on the interior
handle causes the exterior handle to extend from the
airframe. The cargo ramp may be operated regardless of
upper door position.
RAMP CONTROL
Either upper door handle can be used to open and lock the
PANEL
door in the up position. If the ramp or door is unlocked
during ground operations, a RAMP OPEN advisory will
illuminate. If the ramp or door is unlocked in flight, a
RAMP OPEN caution will illuminate.
Sliding Door Configuration
The sliding door configuration provides entrance and exit
for passengers and crewmembers. The upper half of the
door has a large window and slides rearward to open, the
lower half swings inward to the front. The operating
controls are inside and outside rotating handles on both
halves of the door. Operation of the handles are indicated by
the placards on the door/airframe. Both upper and lower
doors can be locked into the open position to facilitate SAR
operations. The upper and lower sections are each
monitored by a microswitch. If either section is unlocked,

LANDING GEAR retract/extend actuator. The main landing gear is mechani-
cally self-locking in both the extended and retracted posi-
The retractable, tricycle, cantilever-type landing gear tions.
consists of a swiveling nose gear and a right and left main
gear. Extension and retraction of the landing gear is electri-
cally controlled through the LDG GEAR control panel.
Normal operation is provided by hydraulic pressure from
the utility hydraulic system. There is also an emergency
pneumatic extension system. Power for the LDG GEAR
control panel and the L N R indicator lights is provided from
the DC Essential bus through circuit breakers marked LG
CTRL and LG POS LTS.
Nose Landing Gear
The nose landing gear consists of a shock strut, dual wheels
and tires on a common shaft and a retract/extend actuator.
The wheel and tire assembly can caster 360° and is
non-steerable.
Shear Fuse Switch
Shock Struts
The shock struts are an oleo-pneumatic type designed to
meet energy absorption requirements for normal and
emergency landings. Each strut contains a device to prevent
ground resonance, an integral axle, hydraulic and pneumatic
servicing ports, and a frangible tube, which absorbs energy
from a hard landing. A shear fuse switch on each shock strut
activates a HARD LANDING caution, indicating that the
shear ring has yielded. The main landing gear struts have
provisions for tiedown rings in the outboard trunnion pins
on the exterior aft sponson. The nose gear strut has a
centering cam, shimmy damper, and axle with spools for
attaching a tow bar.
Main Landing Gear

Single Cue Aircraft Symbol
The single cue symbol resembles the swept wings of an
airplane. The black symbol shows actual aircraft attitude
while the magenta symbol shows the flight director
requested/commanded attitude. The apex or point of the
black symbol is on the actual pitch attitude. Roll attitude can
be determined by comparing the black wings to the
brown/blue horizon line. The magenta flight director symbol
RF31005 is a 9 fly to 9 command. The flight director commands are

Sky/Ground Shading
A blue filled region above the horizon line represents the
sky. A brown filled region below the horizon line represents
PITCH ROLL
FLY-TO FLY-TO the ground. The entire sky/ground representation rotates
INDICATOR INDICATOR around the aircraft symbol to reflect the current roll angle.
The sky/ground shading also translates on a line
perpendicular to itself to represent pitch angle, with transla-
tion reaching a maximum at 6 22° pitch. Sky ground
translation is limited at 6 22° (though the pitch tape and
horizon line are not) in order to ensure the display of some
amount of both sky and ground coloring in all extreme
attitude conditions.

used for the inner marker.
Ground Speed Indication
Ground speed is displayed as a white digital readout below
the airspeed indicator. Ground speed is derived from the
Flight Management System (FMS). If FMS is not installed
or functional, ground speed is derived from the selected
NAV source Distance Measuring Equipment (DME). DME
based ground speed is only accurate when flying directly to
or from the selected station.

Emergency Power Supply (EPS)
The EPS consists of a lead acid battery providing 24 vdc to
power the backup attitude indicator and all standby instru-
ment lighting (attitude indicator, airspeed indicator,
altimeter and compass). If the aircraft power systems fail,
the EPS supplies power to the standby attitude indicator and
standby gage lights for 2 hours. The EPS is constantly
charged by the NO. 1 DC PRI bus through the STDBY ATT
circuit breaker.
The EPS is tested with the BATTERY TEST switch located
to the right of the standby attitude indicator. To test the EPS:

EICAS CAUTIONS EXPLANATION
AC GEN 1 FAIL AC GEN 2 FAIL Generator failure. Set when less than 100 vac detected by the affected
GCU.
Suppressed when aircraft is on the ground and N r , 96%.
AC GCU 1 FAIL AC GCU 2 FAIL Generator control unit failure. Set when the affected under-voltage, over-
current or short circuit protective functions are not working as
determined by continuous built in test (CBIT) or initiated built in test
(IBIT).
ACC 1 CHIP ACC 2 CHIP Accessory chip. Either condition below:
1. Metal particles in the affected accessory module oil. Set by the chip
detection system computer via a magnetic chip plug located in the bot-
tom of the accessory gearbox. Caution delayed 300 milliseconds after
six fuzz burn attempts.
2. Affected accessory module oil temperature above 284°F. Set by the
chip detection system computer via a temperature sensor integral to the
chip plug.
AFCS DGRD Automatic flight control system degraded. One or more faults that limit
the overall function of the AFCS. AFCS DGRD caution may also be
accompanied by either or both AP FAIL cautions.
The AFCS DGRD caution usually involves the higher order features
of the AFCS such as hover augmentation, gust alleviation and
longitudinal stability enhancement. The following AFCS related faults
will set this caution via the affected FCC:
1. Main processor failure. Set by IBIT in the FCC.
2. AHRS rate or attitude signal failure. Set by either of the following:
a. An AHRS invalid status.
b. A miscompare with the other AHRS.
c. The FCC receiving no data from the AHRS.
3. Any longitudinal, lateral or vertical accelerometer failure. Set if the
#1 and #2 systems do not agree or if either system is out of range.
4. Cross channel data link failure. Set when the affected FCC does not
receive communications from the opposite FCC.
5. Any of the four stick position sensors fail. Set when RVDT check
sums do not agree.
6. Either secondary SAS is selected by pilot but is not engaged. Set
when secondary SAS is selected but hydraulic turn on valve is not on.
7. SAS actuator failure. SAS actuator position does not agree with the
position commanded by the FCC.
8. Trim beeper failure. Set when the demanded beeper trim output of the
#1 and #2 systems do not match.
9. The SAS output signal is not received at the actuator. This checks for
broken wires. Set by wrap around logic.
10. SAS servo does not center when turned off. Set only when the af-
fected SAS servos are selected off.
11. Trim actuator failure. Set when actual trim actuator movement does
not correspond with the commanded movement. Includes checks of stick
position, trim position, and spring deflection signals.

12. Airspeed failure. No airspeed sensed by the AFCS. Set when either
ADC is not valid or the two airspeeds are more than 20 knots off above

APU FAIL Auxiliary power unit failure. The APU has automatically shut down due
to any of the following:
The caution will be set by the ESU when on the ground for the follow-
ing conditions:
1. Failure to start. Set when:
a. APU reaches 10% and then dips below 10% during start attempt.
b. APU does not reach governed speed within 70 seconds of start
invocation.
c. APU speed does not reach 5% within 30 seconds of the start invoca-
tion.
d. EGT drops below a set temperature (initial temperature plus 200°F)
for more than 30 seconds during start attempt.
2. Under-speed. Set when APU reaches 95% and then dips below 90%
for more than 10 seconds.
3. Fuel solenoid circuitry fault. Set when a fault is sensed in the fuel
solenoid or it’s circuitry.
4. Fuel torque motor fault. Set when an open or short circuit is detected
or current flow to the circuit is out of range.
5. Loss of EGT signal. Set during the prestart test if no EGT signal is
received or if EGT goes out of range (greater than 2100°F or less than
−180°F).
6. Low oil pressure. Set when the APU reaches 95% and the oil pres-
sure switch is closed for 15 seconds.
7. High oil temperature. Set when oil temperature is greater than 325°F
for one second.
8. High exhaust gas temperature. Set when EGT is greater than a speci-
fied temperature. The allowable temperature is dependent upon APU
speed.
9. Oil temperature sensing fault. Set when an open or short circuit is
detected or the measured oil temperature is out of range (above 375°F
or less than −119°F).
10. Flame out. Set when APU speed is between 5% and 95% and EGT
is less than 275°F for more than 17 seconds.
11. Hung start. Set when a start has been commanded and the APU ac-
celeration is below set values.
The caution will also be set by the ESU at any time (on the ground or
in flight) for the following:
12. Overspeed. Set when APU speed is greater than:
a. 107% as sensed by the hardware overspeed circuit.
b. 109% as sensed by the backup software algorithm.
13. ESU failure.
14. Failure of both the fuel control unit torque motor and shutoff valve.
15. Loss of overspeed protection.

APU FAULT Auxiliary power unit fault. This caution will only occur in flight. The
APU is still running (or trying to start) but the ESU has sensed one of
the following faults:
1. Failure to start. Set when:
a. APU reaches 10% and then dips below 10% during start attempt.
b. APU does not reach governed speed within 70 seconds of start
invocation.
c. APU speed does not reach 5% within 30 seconds of start invocation.
d. EGT drops below a set temperature (initial temperature plus 200°F)
for more than 30 seconds.
2. Under-speed. Set when APU reaches 95% and then dips below 90%
for more than 10 seconds.
3. Fuel solenoid circuitry fault. Set when a fault is sensed in the fuel
solenoid or it’s circuitry.
4. Fuel torque motor fault. Set when an open or short circuit is detected
or current flow to the circuit is out of range.
5. Loss of EGT signal. Set by the ESU during the prestart test or if
EGT is out of range (greater than 2100°F or less than −180°F).
6. Low oil pressure. Set when the APU reaches 95% and the oil pres-
sure switch is closed for 15 seconds.
7. High oil temperature. Set when oil temperature is greater than 325°F
for one second.
8. High exhaust gas temperature. Set when EGT is greater than a speci-
fied temperature. The allowable temperature is dependent upon APU
speed.
9. Oil temperature sensing fault. Set when an open or short circuit is
detected or the measured oil temperature is out of range (above 375°F
or less than −119°F).
10. Flame out. Set when APU speed is between 5% and 95% and EGT
is less than 275°F for more than 17 seconds.
11. Hung start. Set when a start has been commanded and the APU ac-
celeration is below set values.
APU GCU FAIL APU generator control unit failure. Set when the under-voltage, over-
current or short circuit protective functions are not working as
determined by CBIT or IBIT.
APU GEN FAIL APU generator failure. Set when less than 100 vac detected by the APU
GCU.
APU OVERLOAD APU generator overload. Set when all of the following occur:
1. The APU generator is the sole source of electrical power to the
aircraft.
2. The NO 2 ENGINE ANTI-ICE switch is ON.
3. The PLT WDSHLD ANTI-ICE switch is in OVRD.
AUTO DEICE FAIL Automatic deice fail. Automatic mode of deice system failed. Set by the
RIPS controllers when any of the following occur:
1. Internal faults in both RIPS controllers.
2. Failure to receive liquid water content (LWC) data from both ice
detectors.

( AURAL ALERT (

NOTES: Voice Cancel: The voice cancel feature allows the pilot to silence the
active aural alert by pushing the VOICE CNCL button on either cyclic.
Voice cancel works for all continuous aural alerts but only silences the
alert one time per button push.
Audio Inhibit: The audio inhibit feature allows the pilot to silence
selected EGPWS aural alerts for five minutes by selecting AUD INHB
on the MFD. Once audio inhibit is selected, the affected aural alerts will
not be heard for five minutes or until audio inhibit is deselected. This
feature will avoid nuisance aural alerts when the pilot knowingly
conducts operations that would normally elicit EGPWS alerts.
The EGPWS alert explanations presented above do not include all of the
nuances of this complex system. A more thorough discussion of the
EGPWS alerts can be found in the EGPWS MK XXII Pilot’s Guide.

Introduction

PART 2, SECTION I
FUEL SYSTEM
FUEL SYSTEM
Introduction
A separate suction fuel system is provided for each engine.
Fuel is stored in two main crash resistant fuel tanks, one
located in each sponson. These tanks are nylon reinforced
rubber bladders that hold 382 gallons of fuel each, (ap-
proximately 5175 pounds (2347 Kg) total). The fuel system
consists of two prime pumps, two engine prime shutoff
valves, APU fuel shutoff valve, fuel selector valves,
breakaway valves, pressure refueling cross feed tube, and
associated plumbing. A single point pressure
refueling/defueling fitting located on the left side of the
helicopter provides refueling/defueling of both tanks. The
tanks can also be gravity refueled. Fuel from the No. 1 tank
supplies the No. 1 engine and the APU; fuel from the No. 2
tank supplies the No. 2 engine. There are 2.4 gallons of
unusable fuel in each tank.

Each fuel tank has a fuel control switch located on the RF28004

(crossfeed) and DIRECT. In the OFF position the fuel

Standard and Improved Windshield Wipers
There are two types of windshield wipers available. Standard windshield wipers (P/N 92207-01807-103) have an

Four drive shafts connect the MGB module to the TGB. The
shafts drive the MGB oil cooler blower and transmit torque
to the tail rotor.
Tail Drive Shaft
The first drive shaft connects the tail takeoff flange of the
MGB to the input flange of the MGB oil cooler blower
shaft. The second and third drive shafts make up the
horizontal shafts connecting to the IGB. The fourth drive
shaft is larger in diameter and connects the IGB to the TGB.
The drive shafts are connected by flexible couplings and
hanger bearings. Snubber dampers are installed in the
midsection of the #2 and #3 shafts.

CARGO HOOK
Introduction
The cargo hook is used for external load operations and can
support a load of 8,000 pounds (3636 Kg). It consists of the
following components: cargo hook, overhead panel control
switch, cyclic stick release buttons, cockpit and cargo hook
well manual release levers, and cargo hook access door in
the cabin floor. The cargo hook is mounted on the aircraft
center line at station 354 and is accessible from the cabin
through the cargo hook access door. The hook consists of a
load beam, keeper, and both electrical and mechanical
release mechanisms. The cargo hook release can be
activated by the pilot, copilot, or crewmember. There are RF25002
SA
five release controls: an electric cargo release button on
each cyclic stick, a mechanical cargo release handle in the Cargo Hook Switch
cockpit, and two mechanical release levers on the cargo
When not in use, the cargo hook should be placed in the
hook.
stowed position by opening the cargo hook door and pulling
the hook to the right and up. When the hook is in the stowed
Power for the cargo hook is provided by the NO. 2 DC PRI
position the load beam rests on a spring-loaded latch.
bus through circuit breakers marked CRG HOOK CTRL
and CRG HOOK PWR. Power for the cargo hook warning
system is provided by the BATT bus through a circuit
breaker marked CARGO HOOK WARN.
To prepare the cargo hook for operation, open the cargo
hook access door and push down on the latch until the hook
swings into the operating position. In the operating position,
the hook can swivel 30° in all directions. The hook contains
a set of elastomeric bumpers to dampen shock and vibration
from the motion of the load.

RESCUE HOIST
SECONDARY
PENDANT PRIMARY
Introduction
PENDANT
The rescue hoist is electrically powered and controlled with
a capacity of 600 pounds (273 Kg) and speed of up to 325
feet (100 m) per minute. It consists of the following
components: RSQ HST switch on the cockpit MISC SYS
panel, hoist, and hoist operator’s control panel and pendant
in the forward right cabin. The hoist consists of a winch,
electric motor, fan, 200 feet (61 m) or 290 feet (88 m) of
cable with a hook attached to the cable end by a ball bearing
swivel, and a guillotine type cable cutter driven by a
cartridge activated device (CAD). With weight-on-wheels
the hoist is disabled. The hoist motor has built in over-
temperature protection. Temperature sensors in the motor
will illuminate the OVER TEMP caution on the hoist
operator’s control panel and the pendant when the motor
becomes hot. When the temperature falls below the preset
limit the OVER TEMP caution will extinguish. The first and
last 20 feet (6.1 m) of cable are colored bright orange to

PART 2, SECTION II
WEIGHT AND BALANCE
INTRODUCTION FAA/AUTHORITY as satisfying all requirements for
instructions on loading of the rotorcraft within approved
In accordance with FAA/AUTHORITY procedures, the limits of weight and center of gravity, and on maintaining
detail weight and balance data of this section are not subject the loading within such limits.
to FAA/AUTHORITY approval. The loading instructions of
this section, however, have been approved by
Loading Instructions
1. Obtain the current aircraft basic weight and aircraft basic weight moment/1000 from Chart C and enter each in
the appropriate columns of the manifest.
2. Obtain the aircraft takeoff gross weight and moment/1000 by adding, to the current aircraft basic weight and
moment/1000, the weight and moment/1000 of each useful load item to be carried. The weight and moment/1000
of useful load items are shown in Weight Moment Charts (Figures 2-7 through 2-12). Useful load items include fuel,
oil, crew, passengers, baggage and/or cargo. Do not exceed the specified compartment capacities at any time.
3. Determine by reference to the Center of Gravity (C.G.) Chart, Figure 2-1 , that the takeoff gross weight and
moment/1000 obtained is within the recommended weight and C.G. limits.
4. Check that the aircraft will remain within C.G. limits throughout the flight as follows: (a) deduct the weight and
moment/1000 of expendable items (e.g. the fuel), (b) compute the landing gross weight and moment/1000, and (c)
determine by reference to the C.G. Chart, Figure 2-1, if landing gross weight and moment/1000 is within limits. Bring
the aircraft weight and/or balance within limits if either the weight or moment/1000 is outside of the recommended
limits by loading, removing and/or redistributing useful load.
5. Longitudinal C.G. limits are tabulated below and are also shown for reference in Figure 2-2.

vertical takeoff depends upon where in the takeoff sequence Do not select two minute power until

PART 2, SECTION IV
NOISE ABATEMENT
S-92A FLY NEIGHBORLY RECOMMENDATIONS A normal Category A horizontal takeoff is an acceptable
alternative procedure for takeoff noise abatement.

considered as guidelines and should not take Maintain a minimum altitude of 4,000 feet when transit-
